tasks.short: Decide the course topics, write the syllabus, write homework with worked solutions, write handouts, check the final materials, and publish them in the learning system.

steps.what: Mathematics lecturer decides objectives and topics for the course materials
Mathematics lecturer prepares the syllabus with schedule, rooms and assessment dates
Mathematics lecturer writes homework assignments with worked solutions

loop.input: The lecturer's model problem, the learning objective it tests and the course notation.
loop.check: A computer algebra system recomputes each final answer and drops variants whose solution does not match; the lecturer then reads every problem and solution, confirms it tests its objective, and edits or drops it.
loop.stop: Up to five variants per model problem; if none pass, the lecturer writes them.
loop.why_not_simpler: Parameter templates only change numbers; new contexts and twists need drafting.

steps.what: Mathematics lecturer checks the final syllabus, homework and handouts
Mathematics lecturer uploads the materials to the learning system

tasks.design: A syllabus generator fills the schedule, rooms, assessment dates and weights from the course catalogue and timetable, and the lecturer adds the content. A bounded step drafts homework variants from the lecturer's model problems; a computer algebra system checks every answer, and the lecturer reads and edits each problem. Handouts start from a shared course library of earlier handouts. Once checked, the materials are published to the course in the learning system ({LMS}) on set dates.
tasks.previous_blocker: Syllabi were retyped each year and homework written problem by problem.
tasks.enabler_now: Language models draft problem variants that a computer algebra system can check.
tasks.still_hard: Proof questions cannot be checked by a computer algebra system.
tasks.human_edge: Choosing the problem that makes a concept click.
tasks.altitude: The lecturer chooses and checks problems instead of writing every variant.

reach.learn: Whether there are enough practice problems.

evidence.claim: EduGenAI is a chat platform for Dutch universities, in pilot; Utrecht forbids automated grading on it.
Language models can draft problem variants whose answers a computer algebra system can check.
The AI Act's high-risk education points cover evaluating learning outcomes, not preparing course materials.

assumptions: Boundary: from the course due to materials published; teaching is outside.
Input contract: course catalogue and timetable available; fallback is typing.
The lecturer reads every problem and solution.
Proof questions are written by the lecturer.
research_questions: How many drafted problems are kept?

already_counted.description: Mathematics lecturer checks and edits drafted problems.

incremental.description: Mathematics lecturer keeps the model problem library and checking scripts current.

approvals.approved_version: The syllabus, homework and handouts as checked by the lecturer in s5.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: a proof-heavy course; high: a large calculus or statistics course with many computational problems.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Collect course evaluations and pass rates, analyse results per topic, discuss revisions with colleagues, decide changes, and rewrite course descriptions.

steps.what: Mathematics lecturer collects course evaluations and pass rates from several systems
Mathematics lecturer evaluates course content by analysing student results per topic
Mathematics lecturer discusses revisions with colleagues and the curriculum committee
Mathematics lecturer decides revisions to content and methods of instruction
Mathematics lecturer revises the course description and curriculum documents

tasks.design: A course dashboard ({BI}) combines evaluation scores, pass rates and item statistics per learning objective from the assessment tool, so the lecturer does not collect them from several systems or build tables per topic. The course catalogue form opens with last year's text and tracks changes, so only changed parts are rewritten. Discussing and deciding revisions stay with the lecturer and colleagues.
tasks.previous_blocker: Results sat in separate systems and course descriptions were retyped.
tasks.enabler_now: Assessment tools report item statistics; dashboards combine course data.
tasks.human_edge: Seeing why students struggle with a topic.

evidence.claim: The assessment platform used at Erasmus University Rotterdam auto-marks closed questions and reports item statistics.
Course analyses use aggregated student results; personal data need a lawful basis.

assumptions: Boundary: from the course ended to descriptions revised; programme accreditation is outside.
Input contract: items tagged with learning objectives; fallback is spreadsheets.
Revision decisions stay with the lecturer and committee.
research_questions: Do pass rates on weak topics improve after revision?

incremental.description: Mathematics lecturer tags new items with learning objectives.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: a small course with few assessments; high: a large first-year course with many tagged items.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Hold office hours with students, schedule appointments by e-mail, answer repeated questions by e-mail, and note agreed follow-up.

steps.what: Mathematics lecturer maintains office hours to advise and assist students
Mathematics lecturer schedules appointments with students by e-mail
Mathematics lecturer answers repeated course questions by e-mail
Mathematics lecturer notes advice and agreed follow-up

tasks.design: Students book office hour slots themselves in the lecturer's booking page ({CALENDAR}), so appointments are not set by e-mail. A course question page in the learning system ({LMS}) answers the questions that come every year, such as deadlines, allowed calculators and resit rules, so the lecturer answers fewer repeated e-mails. Advising students stays with the lecturer.
tasks.previous_blocker: Appointments and repeated questions were handled one e-mail at a time.
tasks.enabler_now: Booking pages and course question pages are standard tools.
tasks.still_hard: Students still e-mail questions the page answers.
tasks.human_edge: Seeing that a student is stuck on more than mathematics.

reach.learn: Whether slots are easy to book.

evidence.claim: Booking pages let students pick free slots in a calendar.
Notes on students are personal data and need a lawful basis.

assumptions: Boundary: from the student request to follow-up noted; study advice by advisers is outside.
Input contract: booking page linked to the lecturer's calendar; fallback is e-mail.
Students book in about the time an e-mail took.
research_questions: Do more students use office hours?

incremental.description: Mathematics lecturer updates the course question page.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: a small course with few requests; high: a large first-year course with many e-mails.

tasks.short: Prepare discussion questions, moderate the classroom discussion, collect answers by show of hands, and note points for the next lecture.

steps.what: Mathematics lecturer prepares discussion questions and problems
Mathematics lecturer initiates, facilitates and moderates classroom discussions
Mathematics lecturer collects student answers by show of hands and counts them
Mathematics lecturer notes points to revisit in the next lecture

tasks.design: Discussion questions are kept in a shared course question bank ({LMS}) and reused or adapted, instead of being written anew. Students answer multiple-choice questions on their phones in a classroom polling tool that shows the spread at once, so the lecturer does not count hands. Moderating the discussion stays with the lecturer.
tasks.previous_blocker: Questions were written per lecture and answers counted by hand.
tasks.enabler_now: Classroom polling tools show answers at once.
tasks.still_hard: Open questions do not fit a poll.
tasks.human_edge: Drawing a quiet student into the discussion.

reach.learn: Whether anonymous polls get more students to answer.

evidence.claim: Classroom polling tools collect answers from students' phones and show the spread at once.

assumptions: Boundary: from the lecture due to points noted; assessment is outside.
Input contract: polling tool licensed by the university; fallback is a show of hands.

incremental.description: Mathematics lecturer sets up polls per lecture.
Students answer polls on their phones.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: small seminars; high: large lectures with many polls.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The mathematics lecturer keeps choosing problems, deciding revisions, advising students and moderating discussions; retyped syllabi, problem-by-problem writing, scattered results and e-mail scheduling shrink.
skills_to_grow: Checking drafted problems with a computer algebra system
role.ambitious_version: A lecturer with more time with students.
